column4: The brothers' proposal places Joseph in the hidden depth of a well so that a caravan may recover him, establishing the well scene whose bucket appears in 12:19.
Joseph is actually lowered into the well's depth here; this is the human content later drawn out by the water carrier's bucket in 12:19.
God's messenger identifies both God's she-camel and her watering right, a compact parallel to the section's ordered turn at the communal water source.
The righteous drink from a spring which God's servants cause to flow abundantly, joining a drinking vessel's source to deliberate distribution of its water.
All things have their treasuries with God and descend only in a known measure; the ayah supplies a vast source, measured release, and bounded receiving capacity immediately before the water of 15:22.
Clouds are driven together, joined, and made into a mass before rain emerges through them; gathered abundance empties through an outlet like the source dictionary's collected water and bucket-mouth.
Moses declares that he will travel until reaching the meeting of the two seas; this supplies the water-destination within which he later names his نَصَب in 18:62.
At the meeting of the seas the fish takes its path into the water, locating the journey-fatigue stated in 18:62 inside a concrete water scene.

Dhu al-Qarnayn says what his Lord has established for him is better and asks the people to help with strength; divine gift and directed labor initiate the structure that receives poured copper in 18:96.
After Moses waters and petitions his Lord in 28:24, one woman brings an invitation to recompense him for that watering; needed provision arrives through the very act of emptying water for others.
Salsabīl is the named spring behind the Garden's drink, continuing the section's movement from measured cups to an abundant water source.
Tasnim is identified as a spring from which those brought near drink, again placing a privileged drink in relation to its source rather than the cup alone.
God raises clouds, spreads and fragments them, and rain comes from within them; the gathered container releases its provision and its recipients rejoice.
Noah promises that turning to God will bring the sky's water in abundance, making abundant outpouring a gift sought from its Lord.
The abundant rain of 71:11 continues as wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, spelling out the large desirable gift that fills more than bodily thirst.
God sends winds before His mercy and sends pure water from the sky, identifying the giver behind the descending supply.
The water revives dead land and gives drink to cattle and many people, showing what the poured provision fills and restores.
Lofty mountains and sweet water are placed together, a concise Quranic meeting of erected stone mass and life-giving drink.
The promised Garden contains rivers of unspoiled water, milk, wine, and honey, extending the wide basin into an abundance whose contents do not spoil.
Gardens of palms and grapes have springs made to gush within them, making abundant water the interior source of fruit and provision.
The graves are scattered open, a further image of closed earthly containers discharging what was held inside them.
God sends tranquility down into believers' hearts so that faith increases, a positive inner filling comparable to patience poured into a heart emptied by fear.
Believers are told to race toward forgiveness and a Garden as wide as heaven and earth, explicitly identifying that vast capacity as God's bounty.
The command to hasten toward forgiveness and a Garden as wide as the heavens and earth links Godward effort with an expansiveness prepared as reward.
“My earth is spacious, so worship Me” joins width with an exclusive Godward command, paralleling the widened interior's final orientation to its Lord.
The angels pray that their Lord encompasses all things in mercy and knowledge; divine vastness becomes the ground for asking that repentant people be admitted and filled with mercy.
A human being has only what he strives for, supplying the effort that reaches its explicit endpoint with the Lord in 53:42.
وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الْمُنتَهَىٰ names the Lord as the terminus of the striving stated in 53:39, closely matching the sequence of labor followed by Godward direction.
After receiving stone-born springs and divine food, Israel says it cannot endure one food and demands varied produce; appetite rejects the measured gift already filling it.
The people call their companion and he hamstrings the she-camel, violently breaking the apportioned water arrangement announced in 54:28.
The people deny the messenger and hamstring the she-camel, rejecting the watering boundary stated in 91:13 and bringing judgment from their Lord.
The condemned are given drink from a boiling spring, reversing both the desired water source and the restorative drink of the section's wellside scene.
Devouring inheritance with an all-consuming appetite gives a social form to the source dictionary's wide-bellied gluttony.
Intense love of wealth follows voracious consumption in 89:19, showing desire expanding beyond bodily capacity into acquisitiveness.
